questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman presented with lower abdominal pain and bleeding between menstrual periods. She also reported intermittent fevers to 101°F (38.3°C). She had appendicitis age 13 years and had no known drug allergies. She had had unprotected vaginal intercourse with two casual male partners in the past 3 months. On examination, her temperature was 101.2°F (38.4°C), blood pressure 124/82 mmHg, pulse 80/minute, and respiratory rate of 14 breaths/minute, SaO2 98% on room air. A mucopurulent discharge was visible over the cervix, there was cervical motion and adnexal tenderness, and the cervix os bled easily upon application of pressure. NAAT studies were sent for gonorrhea, chlamydia, and trichomoniasis.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric treatment?

options.text: Azithromycin 1 gram orally for one dose
Ceftriaxone 125 mg IM for one dose
Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM stat plus doxycycline 100 mg BID
Metronidazole 2 gram orally for one dose
Metronidazole 500 mg orally BID for 7 days

questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM stat plus doxycycline 100 mg BID In patient with the above clinical constellation, a low threshold to treat empirically for pelvic inflammatory disease should be maintained. Empiric outpatient therapy should cover Gonorrhea, Chlamydia, and anaerobic organisms. Current recommendations are to initiate therapy with one dose of ceftriaxone 250 mg IM plus doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours with follow-up in 3 days for repeat evaluation. Other therapeutic regimens would not adequately cover likely culprit organisms.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q21

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman was 40+2 weeks pregnant. She had a prolonged membrane rupture with multiple vaginal examinations. On exam, her temperature was 39.2°C, and her heart rate was 118 beats/minute. Purulent amniotic fluid was noted.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Ureaplasma urealyticum Chorioamnionitis is usually an ascending polymicrobial infection. All of the options have been implicated in the pathogenesis of chorioamnionitis. However, the most common causative organism is Ureaplasma urealyticum, which causes 47% of cases.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q21

parts.text: 3 clinical findings that prompt empiric antibiotics

cohort_answer.text: A sexually active young woman or woman at risk for STIs who presents with: pelvic or lower abdominal pain, and cervical motion tenderness, uterine or adnexal tenderness, Fever >38.3C

parts.text: What are 2 short-term complications of PID?

cohort_answer.text: Perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh Curtis Syndrome); Tubo-ovarian abscess. (Long term complications: hydrosalpinx, chronic pelvic pain, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, two-fold increase risk of ovarian cancer)

parts.text: What are 3 organisms implicated in PID?

cohort_answer.text: Sexually transmitted: Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, HSV, Trichomonas vaginalis (rare). Endogenous: genital-tract mycoplasmas (Mycoplasma genitalium, Mycoplasma hominis, Ureaplasma urealyticum). Anaerobic: Bacteroides spp., Peptostreptococcus spp., Prevotella spp. Facultative: E. coli, Gardnerella vaginalis, Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus spp.

questions.question: A woman has an IUD and presents with fever, chronic abdominal pain, and malodorous vaginal discharge. A gram stain is shown. CT shows a pelvic mass. [image-based question: gram stain]

parts.text: What is the diagnosis?
What do you recommend the gynecologist immediately do?
What is the initial treatment? Name the drug and route.
What is the duration of the treatment?
If a woman with an IUD has the same gram stain but is asymptomatic, what should be done?

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: PID +/- tubo-ovarian abscess, possibly pelvic actinomycosis pending culture. Immediate: Remove the IUD, surgical removal of mass vs IR aspirate with culture. Initial treatment: Empiric CRO 1g IV daily + doxycycline 100mg BID + metronidazole 500mg BID until well enough for oral stepdown, then metro/doxy for 14 days total, plus actino treatment (amoxil or penicillin, technically IV for 14 days then PO stepdown); actino specific: IV PenG x2 weeks then 6-12 months PO. Asymptomatic: counsel and monitor for symptoms, IUD stays in.

questions.question: 37yo F with IUD in situ with 2 year history of chronic pelvic pain and Pap showing beaded GP bacilli and sulfur granules on biopsy (shown picture). CT shows endometritis and adnexal mass.

parts.text: What is the clinical syndrome
What should the gynecologist do
What is your antibiotic choice including route
What is your duration of antibiotic treatment
What if the patient was asymptomatic but had the same gram stain findings on Pap?

questions.model_answer:
a) Clinical syndrome: pelvic actinomycosis (IUD-associated), a tissue-invasive Actinomyces infection with an inflammatory pelvic/tubo-ovarian mass — beaded gram-positive branching bacilli with sulfur granules are characteristic.
b) Gynecologist should remove the IUD (source of infection) and obtain tissue/cultures to confirm diagnosis; drain/debride the adnexal abscess if needed (surgery may be required for a large mass not responding to antibiotics, though extensive surgery should be avoided if possible since disease usually resolves with prolonged antibiotics once the IUD is removed).
c) Antibiotic choice: high-dose intravenous penicillin G, then transition to oral penicillin (or amoxicillin) once clinically improved.
d) Duration: prolonged course, typically 6–12 months total (weeks of IV therapy followed by months of oral therapy) to ensure eradication given the tendency for actinomycosis to relapse.
e) If asymptomatic with the same Pap findings: Actinomyces-like organisms are found incidentally on Pap smear in 4–8% of IUD users and do not equate to invasive pelvic actinomycosis; no antibiotic treatment or IUD removal is required — observe/monitor for symptoms.
questions.beyond_mandell: Specific antibiotic dose/duration for tissue-invasive pelvic actinomycosis (high-dose IV penicillin G followed by 6-12 months oral penicillin/amoxicillin) reflects standard actinomycosis treatment guidance rather than text explicitly present in this chapter excerpt.

questions.question: PM 24. Lady with an IUD, pelvic pain and foul vaginal discharge growing GPB branching bacilli on swab, picture shown (large clump of blue GPB). [image-based question: gram stain of branching GPB]

parts.text: What is the diagnosis? (1)
What do you tell the OB to do immediately (1)
What one antibiotic to give with route (1)
If someone else has an IUD with GBP and is asymptomatic what would you recommend (1)

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Actinomyces israelii infection. Immediate action: Remove IUD, do pelvic US looking for abscess. Antibiotic: Ampicillin or Pen G (IV). Asymptomatic with ALOs: Part of normal flora - removal of IUD unnecessary unless causing disease (ALOs seen in ~7% of Pap smears in IUCD users; low PPV for pelvic infection; warrants patient education and follow-up, not removal, unless equally suitable contraception can be agreed on).

questions.question: Young girl with copper IUD, 2 years of pelvic pain and now evidence of endometritis, adnexal mass, and peripelvic inflammation.

parts.text: What is the diagnosis?
What should the gynecologist do imminently?
What initial treatment regimen?
What is the recommended duration of treatment?
In an alternative patient, what to do with IUD if asymptomatic and this organism is identified on pap smear?

questions.model_answer:
a) Diagnosis: pelvic actinomycosis (associated with long-term copper IUD use), caused by Actinomyces israelii.
b) Imminent gynecologic step: remove the IUD and send it (plus any tissue/pus obtained) for culture and histopathology to confirm the diagnosis; assess for abscess requiring drainage.
c) Initial treatment regimen: high-dose intravenous penicillin G.
d) Recommended duration: prolonged therapy - IV penicillin for 2-6 weeks followed by oral penicillin (or amoxicillin) to complete a total of 6-12 months.
e) Asymptomatic patient with Actinomyces on Pap smear: remove the IUD; antibiotics are generally not required if the patient remains asymptomatic (monitor clinically; treat only if symptoms develop).

questions.question: Woman with endometriosis and endometritis stemming from and IUD. Gram + rods on staining. CT shows an adnexal inflammatory mass. Showed an image with clue cells.

parts.text: Asked for the diagnosis
What you would do for this patient immediately?
Antibiotic Route
Total duration of therapy
Asked what treatment would be indicated if this were uncomplicated

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: PID +/- tubo-ovarian complex/abscess (polymicrobial, often including Gardnerella); clue cells suggest BV, particularly Gardnerella vaginalis. Immediate action: Beta-HCG to rule out ectopic pregnancy; Chlamydia + gonorrhoeae NAAT prior to Rx, screen for other STIs including HIV; empiric Rx. Abx route/regimen: Cefoxitin 2g IV q6h + Doxycycline 100mg IV BID + Metronidazole 500mg PO BID (alternatives: Clindamycin+gentamicin, Ofloxacin+Metronidazole, Levofloxacin+Metronidazole, Amp/Sulbactam+Doxycycline, Cipro+Doxy+metronidazole); outpatient CTX 250mg IM x1 + doxycycline 100mg PO BID x14d +/- flagyl if BV; inpatient Cefotetan 2g IV q12h OR cefoxitin 2g IV q6h + doxycycline. Duration: 14 days if uncomplicated (up to 4-6 weeks for TOA). Uncomplicated treatment: Ceftriaxone 250mg IM x1 + Doxycycline x14d OR Cefoxitin 2g IM x1 + Probenecid 1g PO x1 + Doxycycline x14d (add flagyl given clue cells/BV)

questions.question: Woman with copper IUD has Pap smear, it shows [picture of messy Gram-positive bacilli]. She has several months of pelvic pain and probably other symptoms too.

parts.text: What is the most likely diagnosis?
What do you recommend that the Gynecologist does?
What is your initial antimicrobial therapy? Include the name and route.
What is the total duration of treatment?
What would you do if the same findings on pap smear were found in a different woman who had a copper IUD but no symptoms?

questions.model_answer:
a) Most likely diagnosis: pelvic actinomycosis (Actinomyces israelii) associated with prolonged copper IUD use.
b) Recommend the gynecologist remove the IUD and obtain tissue/culture to confirm the diagnosis, assessing for a pelvic abscess requiring drainage.
c) Initial antimicrobial therapy: high-dose penicillin G, intravenous route.
d) Total duration of treatment: 6-12 months (IV penicillin for the initial 2-6 weeks, transitioning to oral penicillin or amoxicillin to complete the course).
e) If the same Pap smear finding is seen in an asymptomatic woman with a copper IUD: remove the IUD; no antibiotic treatment is necessary if she remains asymptomatic.
